Seven reasons gesture drawings look off, and how to fix them

After a few sessions you notice your drawings go wrong in familiar ways. Most of those mistakes have a cause and an order of repair. Do not try to fix all seven at once: pick the one you see most often and practise only that for a week.

Written and maintained by: Jeremy

Updated November 10, 2026

1. Time runs out while you draw the face

What it looks like. The head and shoulders look fine but everything below the torso is missing. It happens most in short poses such as 30 seconds.

Why it happens. When we look at a scene with people, our eyes go to faces first and often. Eye-tracking studies have shown this repeatedly. Faces also pack a lot to draw into a small area, so time disappears.

How to fix it.

  • Decide not to draw faces in 30-second and one-minute poses. An egg shape is enough for the head.
  • In the first five seconds, draw one line from head to feet. With that line on the page, the pose survives even if time runs out.

Practice 30 sec × 10 poses · All poses

2. The figure grows as you go down and the feet fall off the page

What it looks like. The head sits nicely near the top of the page, but by the legs you run out of paper. The feet get cut off or the legs shrink.

Why it happens. Drawing from the top down, each part comes out slightly too big and the errors pile up toward the bottom. Drawing courses list it as a classic beginner mistake.

How to fix it.

  • Before any line, mark two dots: one for the top of the head, one for where the feet meet the floor.
  • Then check what falls halfway between the dots. For an upright figure it is usually not the waist but the lower pelvis, around the crotch.

Practice 30 sec × 10 poses · Standing & weight shift

3. The head is too big

What it looks like. The figure looks like a child or a cartoon character. It feels faithful to the photo, but side by side the head is clearly larger.

Why it happens. Attention on the face makes us remember the head as bigger than it is. It shares a root with mistake 1.

How to fix it.

  • Use the head as a ruler. Count the distance from the top of the head to the chin as one unit and see how many units the whole body is.
  • Drawing books often describe an average person as about 7.5 heads tall and an idealized figure as 8. Those numbers are conventions, so counting on the photo in front of you is more accurate than memorizing them. Bending or sitting changes the count a lot.
  • Hold the pencil upright at arm's length, line its tip up with the top of the head, and mark the chin with your thumb. Step that length down the body. Keep the arm equally straight every time or the measurement drifts.

Practice 3 min × 5 poses · Jumping, sport & dance

4. The body looks as stiff as a post

What it looks like. The proportions are right but nothing moves. Different poses of the same person all look alike.

Why it happens. The torso becomes one straight rectangle with limbs attached. In a real body the rib cage and pelvis tilt and twist in different directions.

How to fix it.

  • Before drawing, sketch a short shoulder line and hip line and compare their angles. When someone stands with weight on one leg, the two lines often tilt in opposite directions, a stance known as contrapposto since ancient Greek sculpture.
  • Bend the line of action a little more than the photo. In gesture drawing a bit of exaggeration brings out the movement.

Practice 30 sec × 10 poses · Reaching, bending & twisting

5. A standing figure looks about to fall over

What it looks like. The figure seems to pitch forward or sideways. It is hard to say what is wrong, which makes it the most frustrating mistake.

Why it happens. The relationship between the body and the weight-bearing foot differs from the photo. Drawing both legs as equal posts hides which one holds the body up.

How to fix it.

  • Drop an imaginary vertical line from the middle of the torso to the floor. For a still, standing figure it should land toward the supporting foot, or between the feet when the weight is shared evenly.
  • Many books drop the line from the pit of the neck; some instructors prefer the middle of the torso because it is closer to the real centre of mass. Either way it is a quick check, not a precise measurement.
  • Draw the weight-bearing leg darker and the balancing leg lighter. Mark where the feet touch the floor first, then build the legs on top.

Practice 1 min × 10 poses · Standing & weight shift

For more detail, read 1-minute balance: read the pelvis and supporting foot together.

6. Lines come out fuzzy and layered

What it looks like. Instead of one long line, many short strokes pile up and the outline frays. The drawing looks messy and the form blurs.

Why it happens. Fear of being wrong makes us draw in small checked steps. Often only the wrist moves, so only short strokes come out.

How to fix it.

  • Hold the pencil a little further back and draw from the elbow and shoulder, not the wrist. The wrist suits fine detail; the whole arm suits the big flow of a gesture.
  • Do not erase a wrong line; draw a new one beside it. Keep searching lines light and the right line darker.
  • Warm up by drawing ten long curves in the margin before you start.

Practice 30 sec × 15 poses · All poses

7. You trace only the outer outline

What it looks like. The outline of the clothes is accurate but the body looks flat. Lines tangle where the legs overlap or an arm crosses the body.

Why it happens. We read the photo as a flat shape, and an outline does not tell you what is in front and what is behind.

How to fix it.

  • Before outlining, lightly place the rib cage and pelvis as boxes and the limbs as cylinders.
  • Where two parts overlap, keep the front one's line unbroken and stop the back one's line where it meets it. That T-shaped junction is what tells the eye which part is in front.
  • Poses with many overlaps, such as seated or floor poses, give the fastest results.

Practice 3 min × 5 poses · Floor, kneeling & crouching

3-minute seated pose: find the pelvis and read overlaps explains seated overlaps with a photo.

A 30-second checklist after drawing

After a session, lay the pages out together and answer each question with yes or no. The item with the most "no" answers is next week's practice.

  1. Can you read the pose without a face? (1)
  2. Did head to feet fit on the page? (2)
  3. Did you measure the body in head lengths? (3)
  4. Do the shoulder and hip lines have different angles? (4)
  5. Can you see which foot carries the weight? (5)
  6. Are most lines long, single strokes? (6)
  7. Where forms overlap, is the front line unbroken? (7)

If you are not sure where to start, follow the 30-day gesture drawing routine. It practises the line of action, tilts, balance, and masses and overlaps, one theme per week.
